demos.objective: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
demos.slide: syn-s01: slide 1 of 7; slide 1 of 3 in seg-01
demos.chunks:
[syn-s01-c1] (syn-s01) Lecture 3 | Organizing Data and Object Basics | Sample Course 101
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script: This slide starts our look at how we organize data in everyday life. Think of a music playlist—you put songs in a certain order so you can play them quickly. Or people lining up at a bus stop—they board in the order they arrived. Even the undo button in a text editor works the same way, removing the most recent change first. All of these are simple ways we arrange things so they’re easy to use.

demos.objective: Recognize how data is organized in everyday situations
demos.slide: syn-s02: slide 2 of 7; slide 2 of 3 in seg-01
demos.chunks:
[syn-s02-c1] (syn-s02) Outline | - Organizing data | - Object basics
[syn-p01-c1] (reference) People organize information all the time so it is quick to use. A music playlist keeps songs in a chosen order. People waiting at a bus stop board in the order they arrived. The undo button in a text editor removes the most recent change first.
demos.script: This slide shows two main ideas about how we organize data in daily life. First, we often arrange information so we can find or use it quickly. For example, a music playlist keeps songs in a set order, and people boarding a bus follow the order they arrived in. Second, some systems work like a stack—like the undo button in a text editor, which always removes the most recent change first.

demos.question: Which collection does not allow duplicate items?
demos.options:
A: Bag
B: Set
C: List
D: Stack
demos.misconception: Bag rejects duplicates: Believes a bag keeps only one copy of each item.
demos.chunks:
[syn-s05-c1] (syn-s05) Collections | - Bag | - Set | - List | - Stack | - Queue | - Map
[syn-p03-c2] (reference) A bag holds items in no particular order and allows duplicates. A set holds items in no particular order and does not allow duplicates. A list keeps items in a sequence, and each item has a position.
demos.title: Bags allow duplicates, sets do not
demos.text: A lot of you picked bag, thinking it rejects duplicates. But the lesson says a bag is like a shopping bag—you can toss in two identical apples and both stay. A set is the one that keeps only one copy, like a club guest list that won’t let the same name in twice. So bag is not the right answer here.

demos.question: Which item does a stack remove first?
demos.options:
A: The item added most recently
B: The item added first
C: The smallest item
D: A random item
demos.misconception: Stack works like a queue: Believes a stack removes the oldest item first, as a queue does.
demos.chunks:
[syn-s05-c1] (syn-s05) Collections | - Bag | - Set | - List | - Stack | - Queue | - Map
[syn-p03-c3] (reference) A stack adds and removes items at the same end, so the last item added is the first removed (LIFO). A queue adds items at the back and removes them from the front, so the first item added is the first removed (FIFO). A map stores pairs of a key and a value and finds a value by its key.
demos.title: Stack removes the newest item first
demos.text: A lot of you thought a stack works like a line at the grocery store—first in, first out. But a stack is more like a stack of plates: you always take the top one, which is the last one you put there. The lesson says a stack adds and removes at the same end, so the newest item is the first one out. Queues are the ones that work like grocery lines, not stacks.

demos.chunks:
[syn-s04-c1] ADT and Data Structure | - ADT: the data and its operations | - Says what, not how | - Data structure: an implementation in a language
[syn-p02-c1] An abstract data type (ADT) is a description of a kind of data and the operations allowed on it, for example add, remove, and contains. An ADT says what the operations do. It does not say how the data is kept in memory, and it does not depend on a programming language.
[syn-p02-c2] A data structure is a concrete way to store data in a program, written in a specific language. It implements the operations of an ADT. The same ADT can have several data structures behind it, such as an array-based version and a linked version.
demos.question: Which one does not depend on any programming language?
demos.explanation: Many of you picked this one, and it is an easy mix-up. A data structure is written in a specific language; it is the abstract data type that does not depend on a language.

claims.claim: An abstract data type (ADT) does not depend on a programming language.
claims.quote: It does not depend on a programming language

claims.claim: A data structure is written in a specific language.
